--- title: "From a model to a claim" description: "The whole course applied to one survey, ending in the two paragraphs you would actually write, plus the claims the data will not support, and the bias that cross-validation rewards." order: 6 categories: [interpretation, reproducibility] --- ## From numbers to sentences Everything up to here has produced numbers. A paper needs sentences, and the step between them is where most of the damage is done, not by people who do not understand their model, but by people who understand it and then describe it in the vocabulary a reviewer expects. This page takes the survey through the whole course, writes out the two paragraphs, and then does the more useful thing: lists the claims we cannot make, and demonstrates the one kind of error that no amount of validation will catch. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. The R tab is what produced the tables and figures you see; the Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent, shown for translation rather than executed by the site. Figures stay in R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. It is real code, not pseudocode: it runs against the same files through `python/mlbasic_data.py`, and `python/check-snippets.py` executes every snippet in the site to keep it honest. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly**: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## The analysis, in one place Each step points at where it was argued for. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() # §2: raw -> clean, every decision as code modelling <- survey |> select(abundance, depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3, salinity_psu, substrate, season, longitude, latitude) |> drop_na() model_formula <- abundance ~ s(depth_m, k = 8) + s(temperature_c, k = 8) + s(chlorophyll_mg_m3, k = 8) + s(longitude, latitude, k = 30) + substrate + season + salinity_psu set.seed(9) folds <- vfold_cv(modelling, v = 10) # §7: same folds for every model compared pooled <- map_dfr(folds$splits, \(split) { fitted <- gam(model_formula, family = nb(), data = analysis(split)) held <- assessment(split) tibble(truth = held$abundance, prediction = as.numeric(predict(fitted, held, type = "response"))) }) # §7: pool out-of-fold predictions final <- gam(model_formula, family = nb(), data = modelling) tibble(`cross-validated RMSE` = rmse_vec(pooled$truth, pooled$prediction), `cross-validated R²` = rsq_vec(pooled$truth, pooled$prediction), `mean-only baseline RMSE` = rmse_vec(modelling$abundance, rep(mean(modelling$abundance), nrow(modelling)))) |> mutate(across(everything(), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| cross-validated RMSE| cross-validated R²| mean-only baseline RMSE| |--------------------:|------------------:|-----------------------:| | 4.079| 0.284| 4.819|
::: ::: ## Python ```python import numpy as np import pandas as pd import statsmodels.api as sm import statsmodels.formula.api as smf from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error from sklearn.model_selection import KFold from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() # §2: raw -> clean, every decision as code columns = ["abundance", "depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude"] modelling = survey[columns].dropna().reset_index(drop=True) def spline(column, df, frame): """Knots spanning the whole dataset, so that a fold holding an extreme station can still be scored: patsy refuses to extrapolate.""" return (f"bs({column}, df={df}, lower_bound={frame[column].min()}," f" upper_bound={frame[column].max()})") def spline_formula(frame): # There is no mgcv in Python. A spline basis feeding the same negative # binomial is the closest honest equivalent: the wiggliness comes from the # number of knots rather than from a penalty the fit estimates. return "abundance ~ " + " + ".join([ spline("depth_m", 8, frame), spline("temperature_c", 8, frame), spline("chlorophyll_mg_m3", 8, frame), spline("longitude", 5, frame), spline("latitude", 5, frame), "C(substrate)", "C(season)", "salinity_psu", ]) model_formula = spline_formula(modelling) def negative_binomial(formula, data): dispersion = smf.negativebinomial(formula, data).fit( method="bfgs", maxiter=2000, disp=0).params["alpha"] return smf.glm(formula, data, family=sm.families.NegativeBinomial(alpha=dispersion)).fit() folds = KFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=9) # §7: same folds throughout pooled = pd.concat([ # §7: pool out-of-fold pd.DataFrame({"truth": modelling["abundance"].to_numpy()[held], "prediction": negative_binomial( model_formula, modelling.iloc[rows]).predict( modelling.iloc[held]).to_numpy()}) for rows, held in folds.split(modelling) ], ignore_index=True) final = negative_binomial(model_formula, modelling) pd.DataFrame({ "cross-validated RMSE": [root_mean_squared_error(pooled["truth"], pooled["prediction"])], "cross-validated R²": [np.corrcoef(pooled["truth"], pooled["prediction"])[0, 1] ** 2], "mean-only baseline RMSE": [root_mean_squared_error( modelling["abundance"], np.repeat(modelling["abundance"].mean(), len(modelling)))], }).round(3) ``` ::: The `s(longitude, latitude)` term is there because §6 found spatial structure that no covariate explains; the negative binomial because §6 found the counts over-dispersed; the smooth terms because §3 and §10 found the responses humped; and the model family because [the comparison on page 3](black-box-or-not.qmd) put it ahead of a random forest and a boosted tree on these folds. ## The Methods paragraph > Abundance was modelled as a function of depth, bottom temperature, chlorophyll > concentration, salinity, substrate type and season using a generalised additive model with > a negative-binomial response (`mgcv` 1.9.4, R 4.6.1). Depth, temperature and chlorophyll > entered as thin-plate smooths with a basis dimension of 8, and an isotropic smooth of > longitude and latitude (basis dimension 30) was included to absorb spatial structure not > explained by the covariates. Predictive performance was assessed by ten-fold > cross-validation with out-of-fold predictions pooled before scoring, and the same folds > were used for every candidate model compared. Three alternatives (a random forest, a > gradient-boosted tree ensemble and a negative-binomial GLM with quadratic terms) were > fitted for comparison and are reported in the supplement. Analysis code, the package > lockfile and the cleaning script are archived at [DOI]; all random seeds are set in the > code. Every clause there is either a decision the course argued for or a number a reader can check. Note what it does *not* contain: no claim that the model was "validated", no accuracy figure without a baseline, and no silence about the models that lost. ## The Results paragraph ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(final)$s.table |> as_tibble(rownames = "smooth term") |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) signif(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|smooth term | edf| Ref.df| Chi.sq| p-value| |:---------------------|-----:|------:|------:|-------:| |s(depth_m) | 3.29| 4.10| 8.84| 0.06090| |s(temperature_c) | 4.64| 5.55| 116.00| 0.00000| |s(chlorophyll_mg_m3) | 1.00| 1.00| 6.44| 0.01130| |s(longitude,latitude) | 10.70| 14.80| 35.50| 0.00193|
::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(final)$p.table |> as_tibble(rownames = "term") |> filter(str_detect(term, "substrate|salinity")) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | Estimate| Std. Error| z value| Pr(>|z|)| |:-------------|--------:|----------:|-------:|------------------:| |substratemud | 0.170| 0.109| 1.564| 0.118| |substraterock | -0.479| 0.177| -2.712| 0.007| |substratesand | -0.237| 0.109| -2.177| 0.029| |salinity_psu | 0.064| 0.121| 0.527| 0.598|
::: ::: ## Python ```python terms = [t for t in final.params.index if "C(substrate)" in t or "salinity" in t] pd.DataFrame({ "term": terms, "Estimate": final.params[terms].to_numpy(), "Std. Error": final.bse[terms].to_numpy(), "z value": final.tvalues[terms].to_numpy(), "p-value": final.pvalues[terms].to_numpy(), }).round(3) ``` ::: > The model explained substantially more variation than a no-skill baseline > (cross-validated RMSE 4.08 against 4.82 for predicting the survey mean; cross-validated > R² 0.28). Bottom temperature was the strongest predictor, with a clearly non-linear effect > (4.6 effective degrees of freedom, $\chi^2$ = 116, $p < 0.001$) peaking at approximately > 8 °C. Chlorophyll concentration had a positive effect that the model resolved as linear on > the log scale (1.0 e.d.f., $p = 0.011$). Substrate type was associated with abundance, > which was lower on rock than on gravel (−0.48 ± 0.18 on the log scale, $p = 0.007$) and on > sand (−0.24 ± 0.11, $p = 0.029$); mud did not differ detectably from gravel. The spatial > smooth was retained with 10.7 effective degrees of freedom ($p = 0.002$), indicating > structure the measured covariates do not account for. Salinity showed no detectable effect > (0.06 ± 0.12, $p = 0.60$). Depth showed a weak unimodal tendency peaking near 50 m that was > not statistically distinguishable from no effect ($p = 0.061$); we do not interpret it > further, for the reason given below. Four things that paragraph does deliberately. It gives the baseline next to the score. It reports the *shape* of the temperature effect, not only its significance. It reports salinity's null result rather than omitting it. And it declines to interpret depth. ## The claims we cannot make This is the section most papers do not have, and it is the one this course has spent ten sections earning. **We cannot claim a depth optimum.** The true optimum is at 80 m. The GAM's smooth peaks at 52 m, the random forest's partial dependence declines monotonically, and a GLM given the generator's exact functional form estimates the depth quadratic at a fourteenth of its true value. [Depth and temperature are confounded by the sampling design](partial-effects.qmd): there are almost no cold shallow stations and almost no warm deep ones. No model can separate them, and the honest sentence is *"the survey does not separate the effects of depth and temperature"*. **We cannot claim chlorophyll is or is not important.** The GAM finds it significant at $p = 0.011$; permutation importance puts it inside the noise band on one split and first on another, [swinging from rank 1 to rank 11 across eight splits](feature-importance.qmd), because depth and season between them reconstruct most of it. **We cannot claim anything causal.** The model is a description of how abundance co-varies with what happened to be measured, on the stations that happened to be visited. That the temperature effect nearly matches the generator here is a fact about a world we wrote. **We cannot claim it will transfer.** The [conformal coverage on page 5](communicating-uncertainty.qmd) dropped from 96% to 86% when the model was calibrated on low-chlorophyll stations and asked about high-chlorophyll ones, with no change in the interval width to warn us. Outside the sampled envelope there is no guarantee, and §6 says the same about the model itself. **We cannot report the uncertainty the software prints.** Seven models were compared before this one was chosen, so the intervals above are conditional on a selection step they do not account for ([§7](../07-validation/cross-validation.qmd)). ## The error validation cannot catch Every safeguard in this course compares a model against the data. If the data itself is biased, all of them pass. Dredges and grabs catch poorly on hard substrate; this is a well-known gear effect, not a hypothetical one. Suppose our gear recovered only half the animals present on rock. The recorded counts on rock would be halved, everything else unchanged. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(77) biased <- modelling |> mutate(abundance = if_else(substrate == "rock", rbinom(n(), abundance, 0.5), abundance)) compare <- function(data, label) { set.seed(9) out_of_fold <- map_dfr(vfold_cv(data, v = 10)$splits, \(split) { fitted <- gam(model_formula, family = nb(), data = analysis(split)) held <- assessment(split) tibble(truth = held$abundance, prediction = as.numeric(predict(fitted, held, type = "response"))) }) full <- gam(model_formula, family = nb(), data = data) tibble(dataset = label, `CV RMSE` = rmse_vec(out_of_fold$truth, out_of_fold$prediction), `CV R²` = rsq_vec(out_of_fold$truth, out_of_fold$prediction), `rock effect` = coef(full)[["substraterock"]], `std. error` = sqrt(diag(vcov(full)))[["substraterock"]]) } bind_rows(compare(modelling, "as recorded"), compare(biased, "gear halves the catch on rock")) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|dataset | CV RMSE| CV R²| rock effect| std. error| |:-----------------------------|-------:|-----:|-----------:|----------:| |as recorded | 4.079| 0.284| -0.479| 0.177| |gear halves the catch on rock | 4.008| 0.297| -1.164| 0.196|
::: ::: ## Python ```python rng = np.random.default_rng(77) biased = modelling.copy() on_rock = biased["substrate"] == "rock" biased.loc[on_rock, "abundance"] = rng.binomial( biased.loc[on_rock, "abundance"].to_numpy(), 0.5) def compare(data, label): out_of_fold = pd.concat([ pd.DataFrame({"truth": data["abundance"].to_numpy()[held], "prediction": negative_binomial( model_formula, data.iloc[rows]).predict( data.iloc[held]).to_numpy()}) for rows, held in KFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=9).split(data) ], ignore_index=True) full = negative_binomial(model_formula, data) rock = [t for t in full.params.index if "rock" in t][0] return { "dataset": label, "CV RMSE": root_mean_squared_error(out_of_fold["truth"], out_of_fold["prediction"]), "CV R²": np.corrcoef(out_of_fold["truth"], out_of_fold["prediction"])[0, 1] ** 2, "rock effect": full.params[rock], "std. error": full.bse[rock], } pd.DataFrame([compare(modelling, "as recorded"), compare(biased, "gear halves the catch on rock")]).round(3) ``` ::: The estimated rock effect more than doubles, from −0.48 to −1.16. On the count scale that is the difference between "rock holds about 38% fewer animals than gravel" and "rock holds about 69% fewer", and the second sentence is the one that would be written up, with a $p$ value of well under 0.001 behind it. Now look at the validation columns. The biased model **scores better on both**: cross-validated RMSE 4.008 against 4.079, R² 0.297 against 0.284. Not a warning anywhere, but a modest improvement. That is not a fluke, it is structural. Cross-validation asks whether the model predicts the data, and the biased model predicts the biased data very well. The held-out fold carries the same bias as the training folds. There is no resampling scheme, no metric and no interpretation method in this course that detects it. ::: {.callout-important} **The only defences against observation bias are outside the model.** Knowing your gear's catchability by substrate. Comparing against an independent method: video, acoustics, a different net. Reporting the effort and the gear alongside the result so a reader can apply their own correction. A model that reproduces biased survey data reproduces the bias, with excellent validation statistics, and says nothing at all about it. ::: ## Before you submit The reporting checklist is on [the reproducibility page](reproducibility.qmd). Three questions to add to it, all of which this page has answered for the survey: 1. **What is my baseline?** A score without one is not a result. 2. **Which of my claims is not identified by my design?** Write that sentence down before a reviewer writes it for you. 3. **How would my data be biased if my method were imperfect, and would I be able to tell?** ::: {.callout-tip} ## Key points - Write the **baseline next to the score**, the **shape** of an effect rather than only its significance, and the **null results** rather than omitting them. - List the claims the design does not support. On this survey that is the depth optimum, chlorophyll's importance, anything causal, and transfer beyond the sampled envelope. - Uncertainty after a model search is wider than the software prints, because the search is not in the interval. - **Observation bias is invisible to validation.** Halving the recorded catch on rock more than doubled the estimated rock effect and *improved* the cross-validated RMSE and R². - The defences against that are gear calibration, an independent method, and transparent reporting of effort, not a better model. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Bias the data the other way, supposing the gear over-counts in high chlorophyll because of fouling, and check whether cross-validation notices. Then check whether the chlorophyll smooth changes sign. 2. Write the Results paragraph for the random forest instead. Which of the five sentences can you still write, and what do you have to replace them with?
